prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, which have brought the measurement of time and frequency to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize part on B037, Katori and Ye. The achievement is bounded and identifiable: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift of the clock transition while many atoms are interrogated in a Lamb-Dicke confined lattice, and Ye's group carried strontium lattice clocks to the 10^-18 regime of accuracy and stability, including the many-body and cavity-enhanced extensions. It has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories, and the consequences are already measured, not promised: centimetre-scale gravitational redshift tests, bounds on drifts of constants and on ultralight dark matter, and the evidence base for a redefinition of the second. In answer to the chair's novelty question, I would name the new principle explicitly as the magic-wavelength condition: state-insensitive trapping of a large ensemble at a wavelength where the clock transition is unperturbed. That idea is not contained in the comb (2005), which provided the frequency ruler, or in single-ion control and ion clocks (2012), which are limited by a single quantum absorber. The citation should stay narrow and tied to that idea. What changed since round 1 is not the choice but how I weigh it: my opening support for B008 is discounted for reasons given in the conflict note, and the exchange showed that the credit problems on B042, B029 and B006 are more structural than the lattice-clock credit.
statement.case_against: Two reservations remain. First, the AMO and precision-measurement thread has been honoured several times (2005, 2012, and neighbouring prizes), and a committee may reasonably ask for distance. I think the lattice clock is a distinct achievement, but this is a judgment about perceived novelty that I cannot fully remove. Second, a two-name prize leaves out groups at NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and elsewhere, and Boyd, Ludlow and others in Ye's own group, as well as the ion-clock community. A narrow citation and acknowledgement of these contributions in the committee's text is the honest way to handle this; it does not make the credit complete. I also withdraw a factual premise in my round-1 statement: the 2005 prize went to Hall and Hansch for the frequency comb, not to Ye, and I should not have described Ye as sharing it. Ye's comb-era work is context for his later clock work, and nothing more.

responses.point: Pearce keeps B042 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first for its direct chain from prediction to HgTe observation and twenty years of independent confirmation, and accepts the credit gap as the main weakness; in the chair's summary he also corrects his own round-1 premise about Ye and the 2005 prize.
responses.response: I appreciate the correction on the 2005 prize, and I withdraw the same error from my own round-1 statement. That removes the main reason you placed B037 sixth, and I would ask whether your remaining reservation is then only that the lattice clock is an advance in measurement. On B042 I still agree the science is mature, but a citation that credits the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation while the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal tested by that experiment is left out, with Zhang deceased and the 3D work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan also outside, is a prize whose omissions the committee would have to apologise for in the same text. Narrow wording helps but does not repair that. In contrast, the omissions on B037 are groups that reproduced and extended a clock, not the originators of the idea. I will keep B042 as my first alternative, and I would move to it only if the committee could show a principled three-name solution that includes the HgTe proposal.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from the Higgs observation (B006) to B037 because the Katori-Ye credit is the one nobody calls unresolved, but says he is less able to judge experimental priority and that B006 remains the more fundamental discovery.
responses.response: I agree that B006 is the more fundamental discovery, and I do not think a precision-metrology prize should be read as outranking it in significance. Our statutes ask for a discovery or invention and for identifiable people, and on that second criterion the Higgs cannot presently be a three-name prize without being arbitrary; several of us, including you, now say so. If the committee found an expert view on which individuals were decisive, I would reconsider, but no member has supplied one in round 1. On priority in the lattice clock, I can offer a theorist's check on what you asked Lindroth and Kroll to judge: the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice demonstration trace to Katori, and the later accuracy record in strontium traces to Ye's group. Both claims are visible in the independent literature, so I think you can rely on them without needing the finer history.

responses.point: Eriksson moved B042 to the head of his configuration because the theory-plus-experiment trio is coherent and the field reaches into materials and band theory, and in his reply to me he agreed that the graphene spin-orbit gap is tiny so the citation should be tied to the Z2 concept and HgTe, not to graphene.
responses.response: I accept your reply on the graphene gap and agree the Z2 invariant and helical edge states are the conceptual discovery, not the material. That is why I regard the B042 science as strong. Where I still differ is that the trio is called coherent, yet you yourself list Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and the 3D work, as omissions that cannot be repaired later. A citation worded around the Z2 prediction and the HgTe observation is accurate, but the HgTe experiment was designed from the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, so the experimental half rests on work credited elsewhere. Add that the 2016 prize on topological phases sits next to it and that the edge quantisation is less clean, and I cannot rank it above B037. I would support B042 as a worthy later prize if the credit could be settled.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B005 (Toner, Ramaswamy, Vicsek) for conceptual novelty and no previous prize on nonequilibrium collective phenomena, and asks what new physical principle the lattice clock adds beyond the magic-wavelength idea, while admitting that Tu's omission is a real defect.
responses.response: The magic-wavelength condition is the new principle, and I would argue it is more than technique: it makes it possible to hold a many-body ensemble of atoms in a state where the clock transition is unperturbed, and that is what changes the statistics and then the many-body physics available to the clock. Your question is fair, and the citation should say so and not just cite precision. On B005 I find the concept attractive and I agree that the generality of the idea is a good sign. However, you list the omission of Tu, Simha, Marchetti and others as a real defect, and you note that the two-dimensional exponents are still contested. I take those two points together as showing that the prize would rest on a claim not yet settled by experiment and a credit set that is not defensible. I am not able to judge the active-matter literature as well as you, so I do not claim more than that.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B037 first, regards the atomic-structure physics of magic wavelengths and clock shifts as well understood, and in her reply to me weighs circuit QED (B008) and the Cirac-Zoller proposals (B029) below the clock because of the 2022 and 2025 prizes and unclear experimental credit.
responses.response: I agree with your reasoning, and your point on B008 is what I would expect of a committee asked about timing: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits is recent, and I should not use this discussion to push my own subfield. I also agree that B029 has an unclear experimental credit, since Wineland is already honoured and Monroe and others are central. I keep it as a second alternative, because the Cirac-Zoller proposal is a genuine theoretical idea with a long and mature experimental record, but I do not put it in my preferred configuration. Where I would add to your atomic-structure check is the remaining uncertainty on systematic shifts: the 10^-18 claims depend on blackbody radiation shifts and lattice-induced effects, which you can judge better than I can. If you consider those fully controlled, as you say, that settles the maturity question for me.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the lattice clock as a distinct invention or as a further step in the precision-spectroscopy thread honoured in 2005 and 2012.

Whether the pending redefinition of the second is better treated as confirmation of maturity or as a reason to wait; I lean to confirmation, but I cannot rule out that colleagues will see it differently.
How the committee should acknowledge NIST, PTB, SYRTE, RIKEN and others, and Ye's own group members, outside a two-name prize.
Whether B042 can be given a defensible credit given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang (deceased), Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan, and whether the 2016 prize overlaps enough to count against it.
How much distance the committee wants from the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize before considering B008, and how far my own affiliation biases my view of it.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers on superconducting circuits and circuit/waveguide QED, so B008 (circuit QED) is directly in my own subfield; I rely on the committee to discount any view I express on it, and I do not put it forward. Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work on related physics. My profile records no connection to Katori or Ye (B037), to the B042 candidates, or to the B029 candidates, so I see no conflict for my preferred configuration.
